title: Kannappa and the living temple
hookLine: a hunter and a priest care for the same god, and the god bleeds
carry: after prana pratishtha, the god lives there
tomorrow: do you have to give up enjoying life to be free?

lines: A HUNTER, A LINGA, NO TRAINING.
THE PRIEST CLEANS UP. WHO'S RIGHT?
cards: In the hills of Kalahasti, a young hunter named Thinnan finds a Shiva linga alone in the forest, and falls in love. He has no training. So he does what he can.
He carries water in his own mouth to bathe it, wears flowers in his hair to offer it, and brings it meat he's tasted first, to be sure it's good.
Every morning the temple priest arrives, finds the shrine a mess, cleans it and does the proper rites, in order. Every evening the hunter comes back. Who's doing it right?

teach.b: The Periya Puranam, the Tamil lives of the Shaiva saints, tells how Shiva answered. He told the priest to hide and watch. Then blood began to flow from one eye of the linga.
The hunter cut out his own eye and set it there, and the bleeding stopped. When the other eye bled, he put his foot on the spot to find it, and reached for his second eye. Shiva stopped his hand.

From then on he's called Kannappa, for the eye he gave. Notice what both men believed: that the god in that stone was alive enough to thirst, and to bleed. That's the teaching behind every Hindu temple.
When an image is installed, a rite called prana pratishtha, establishing the breath, invites the deity to live in it. From then on the god is a living presence, cared for like an honored guest.
Texts called the Agamas, in tantra's own family, order that care: in many temples, a bell before sunrise, then waking, bathing, dressing, food, lamps, and rest at night.
The priest kept the order; Kannappa had the love the order exists for, and in the story Shiva honors both.
That's why temples keep their hours, morning after morning: someone is there.

how: In temples that follow the Agamas, priests perform the daily rites in a set order: waking the deity, bathing, dressing, offering food and lamps, and evening rest.

o: a yearly festival held at the largest temples
the Agamas: manuals ordering a temple's daily care

games.q: a new temple's image has just been carved, and a neighbor asks why daily worship hasn't started. by the Agamas, what's still missing?
o: prana pratishtha, the rite that invites the deity to live there.
a crowd; worship begins once enough people come to see it.
the paint; worship waits until the image is fully decorated.
games.why: before prana pratishtha, it's a sculpture. after it, the deity is invited to dwell, and the daily rounds of care begin.

practice: In many homes the morning shrine begins like a temple's: a bell or a lamp, a little water, a flower. If you pray, offer one small thing today, as to someone truly there.
If you don't, bring to mind one person you look after, and walk through tomorrow's steps for them, one per breath, as for an honored guest.

wordCard.voice: What tantra actually is: here, the Agamas and prana pratishtha: a god invited to live in a temple, and cared for every day.

orig.note: Sanskrit agama, a teaching handed down; the name of the texts that order temple worship.

carryVoice: Pocket this: after prana pratishtha, the god lives there. Kannappa never doubted someone was there. Day sixteen-fifteen.
